narrative:
FIRST WARN FORECAST
Wednesday, September 2, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

DANGEROUS HEAT CONTINUES THROUGH SATURDAY

There is still no immediate relief from the prolonged late-season heat across Missouri and Illinois.

The Heat Advisory has been extended through Saturday evening for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area as temperatures continue to reach the middle and upper 90s, with some locations approaching 100 degrees. Afternoon heat index values will generally range from 98 to 106 degrees.

The duration of this heat remains an important part of the forecast. We have already experienced several consecutive days of temperatures well above normal, and significant heat will continue through Saturday.

Some relief is expected Sunday following the passage of a weak cold front, although temperatures will remain warmer than normal into early next week.

ANOTHER VERY HOT WEDNESDAY

The large area of high pressure responsible for our late-season heat remains firmly established across the region.

At the surface, high pressure is centered across the eastern United States while a frontal boundary remains well to our north across Iowa and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, the upper-level ridge responsible for the hot and dry weather is centered across Kentucky and Tennessee and will gradually rebuild westward.

Temperatures several thousand feet above the surface remain exceptionally warm for early September, running above the 90th percentile for this time of year.

That will translate into another afternoon of widespread middle and upper 90s across central Missouri, the St. Louis metropolitan area, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois.

A few locations may approach 100 degrees.

Humidity will decrease somewhat during the afternoon as the atmosphere mixes deeply, but it will not be enough to prevent dangerous heat index values.

Expect afternoon heat indices generally between 98 and 106 degrees.

ST. LOUIS URBAN HEAT IS ESPECIALLY NOTICEABLE AT NIGHT

One notable feature of this heat wave has been the difference between rural areas and the St. Louis metropolitan area during the overnight hours.

Early this morning, temperatures have fallen into the 70s across many rural communities while portions of the St. Louis urban core remain in the 80s.

This is the urban heat island effect.

Concrete, asphalt, buildings, and other developed surfaces absorb tremendous amounts of heat during the day and release that heat slowly overnight. As a result, heavily developed areas can remain considerably warmer than surrounding rural communities.

That becomes particularly important during a prolonged heat wave because nighttime temperatures provide the body an opportunity to recover from daytime heat.

For some locations in the St. Louis metro, that overnight relief will remain limited.

THURSDAY BRINGS MORE OF THE SAME

Unfortunately, there is very little change expected Thursday.

The upper-level ridge will remain strong across the central United States, while temperatures several thousand feet above us remain exceptionally warm.

Afternoon highs will once again reach the middle to upper 90s, with isolated locations potentially nearing 100 degrees.

Heat index values should again range from approximately 98 to 106 degrees.

Conditions will remain predominantly dry, and widespread cloud cover or rainfall will not be available to provide meaningful relief.

FRIDAY AND SATURDAY REMAIN DANGEROUSLY HOT

The heat continues Friday and Saturday.

Our upper-level winds will gradually become more northwesterly as the ridge shifts, but the hottest air will remain over Missouri and Illinois long enough to keep temperatures well into the 90s through Saturday afternoon.

That is why the Heat Advisory has been extended through Saturday evening.

Current guidance has also become increasingly consistent regarding Saturday's temperatures. Confidence is fairly high that another afternoon of significant heat will occur before a weak cold front finally begins moving through the region Saturday night.

There is some uncertainty Saturday because thunderstorms could potentially complicate the temperature forecast.

A few computer models suggest a complex of thunderstorms could move southeastward into portions of Missouri and Illinois sometime Saturday. Approximately 20 to 35 percent of our longer-range ensemble guidance currently produces rainfall around the St. Louis region during the weekend.

If thunderstorms develop earlier in the day, clouds and rain could temporarily lower temperatures.

However, there is another side to that possibility.

As the cold front approaches, moisture may pool along and ahead of the boundary. That could push dewpoints higher and make the air more humid. So even if actual temperatures come down a few degrees, the additional humidity could keep heat index values elevated.

For now, the safest forecast is to plan on dangerous heat continuing through Saturday.

SOME RELIEF ARRIVES SUNDAY

Sunday finally offers some improvement.

A weak cold front should move through the region Saturday night, allowing both temperatures and humidity to decrease somewhat.

The change will not exactly feel like fall.

High temperatures are still expected to reach the 90s across much of the region Sunday, but lower dewpoints should help keep heat index values below 100 degrees and below Heat Advisory criteria.

After nearly a week of heat indices around or above 100 degrees, even that modest decrease should be noticeable.

The timing and strength of Saturday night's front will determine exactly how much relief we experience Sunday.

STILL WARM NEXT WEEK

Do not expect a major transition to cool September weather behind this front.

The upper-level ridge is expected to begin rebuilding across the Midwest early next week.

High temperatures Monday and Tuesday are still forecast to reach the 90s.

The difference should be humidity.

Lower dewpoints are expected to keep heat index values below 100 degrees, making conditions somewhat more tolerable than what we are experiencing this week.

Rain chances also appear limited early next week. Fewer than 20 percent of our longer-range ensemble members currently produce measurable rainfall as the ridge begins strengthening again.

HEAT SAFETY REMAINS IMPORTANT

After several consecutive days of extreme temperatures, heat stress can become cumulative.

Continue drinking plenty of water throughout the day and take frequent breaks if you are working or exercising outdoors. Whenever possible, move strenuous outdoor activities to the morning or evening hours.

Check on older family members, friends, and neighbors, particularly anyone without reliable air conditioning.

Remember pets as well. Provide plenty of fresh water and shade, and be cautious with afternoon walks because pavement temperatures can become dangerously hot.

Never leave children or animals inside a parked vehicle.

THE BOTTOM LINE

A Heat Advisory remains in effect across the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Saturday evening.

Wednesday and Thursday will bring widespread middle and upper 90s, with a few locations potentially approaching 100 degrees. Afternoon heat index values will generally range from 98 to 106 degrees.

Very little improvement is expected Friday or Saturday, with dangerous heat continuing across central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois.

There is a chance for thunderstorms around the region Saturday as a weak cold front approaches, but confidence in widespread rainfall remains relatively low.

The front should move through Saturday night, bringing some relief Sunday. Temperatures will still reach the 90s, but slightly cooler air and lower humidity should finally push heat index values below advisory criteria.

Warm weather continues into early next week, although heat index values are currently expected to remain below 100 degrees.

Meteorological fall may have started Tuesday, but the first week of September continues to look and feel very much like summer.

Stay hydrated, limit prolonged exposure during the hottest part of the afternoon, and continue taking this extended period of dangerous heat seriously.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
